question: Why do type hints matter in Python even though the language doesn't enforce them at runtime?
expected_answer_text: Python is dynamically typed — you can assign any value to any variable and Python will not complain. Type hints let you annotate your code with type information so that tools (PyCharm, mypy) and other developers know what to expect.
answer_key: Type hints let you annotate your code with type information

question: What's the relationship between dataclasses and the JSON that Ollama expects?
expected_answer_text: Dataclasses are your internal world. Ollama speaks JSON (plain dicts). build_messages() is the bridge between them.
answer_key: build_messages() is the bridge between them

question: What does the if __name__ == "__main__": pattern actually control?
expected_answer_text: This is one of the most important Python patterns. It controls what runs automatically when a file is executed directly vs when it is imported by another file.
answer_key: It controls what runs automatically when a file is executed directly vs when it is imported by another file

question: What's scheduled right after Day 01 in Week 01?
expected_answer_text: Next up: Day 02 — Virtual Environments & Packaging. pyproject.toml, src/ layout, pip install -e .
answer_key: Next up: Day 02 — Virtual Environments & Packaging
notes: logistics/meta sentence, not a concept explanation -- sits at the very end of the document, good boundary-case test

question: Why does an AI Engineer role fit someone coming from a software engineering background, according to the career analysis?
expected_answer_text: AI Engineer is the most code-heavy, product-oriented AI role — the closest to what you already do.
answer_key: AI Engineer is the most code-heavy, product-oriented AI role
notes: SECTION 1, under a bold-Normal styled sub-heading, not a real Word heading style

question: How is the AI Engineer role defined, compared to a Data Engineer, in the role breakdown?
expected_answer_text: AI Engineer: Connects AI models (LLMs, APIs) to real products and systems. Builds the tools, pipelines, and integrations that make AI useful. Closest to traditional software engineering.
answer_key: Connects AI models (LLMs, APIs) to real products and systems

question: Why does an Ollama install via Homebrew sometimes fail to be found on Apple Silicon?
expected_answer_text: Homebrew on Apple Silicon installs to /opt/homebrew/ — not the default PATH. You hit this issue when ollama was not found after installation.
answer_key: Homebrew on Apple Silicon installs to /opt/homebrew/ — not the default PATH
notes: SECTION 7, far from SECTION 1 -- spread test across the messiest document

question: What's the trim-guard condition in chunk_fixed_size(), and why does it exist?
expected_answer_text: uses a trim-guard (drop the trailing chunk when its remainder is <= o tokens, proven mathematically equivalent to "is the last chunk fully contained in the previous chunk" across roughly 9800 combinations with 0 mismatches) to avoid emitting a near-duplicate final chunk
answer_key: drop the trailing chunk when its remainder is <= o tokens
notes: mid-sentence substring inside a long bullet, not the whole bullet -- tests partial-match retrieval

question: What does "golden" mean in golden_qa.json, and why can it be trusted?
expected_answer_text: golden_qa.json is a hand-labeled reference set: (question, correct answer location) pairs trusted completely, because they're written by hand against real notes. "Golden" means exactly that -- this is the standard everything else gets measured against, not something the system produces and you hope is right.
answer_key: a hand-labeled reference set: (question, correct answer location) pairs trusted completely
notes: replaced 2026-10-13 (W16D01): old q009 pointed at the WHERE I LEFT OFF box, whose text no longer exists

question: Why can splitting a document into non-overlapping fixed windows hurt retrieval later?
expected_answer_text: Splitting a token list into fixed windows with no overlap can cut an important sentence exactly in half across a chunk boundary -- neither resulting chunk contains the whole sentence, which hurts retrieval later (each chunk gets embedded separately).
answer_key: can cut an important sentence exactly in half across a chunk boundary

question: What's the formula for how far a chunk's start position advances each step, given n and o?
expected_answer_text: Each chunk's start must be n - o tokens after the previous chunk's start -- you advance n tokens per chunk, then pull back o tokens for the overlap, netting n - o forward progress each time.
answer_key: you advance n tokens per chunk, then pull back o tokens for the overlap

question: When chunk_fixed_size() is used as a fallback sub-splitter, what open design question does it raise about chunk_index?
expected_answer_text: How do you distinguish sub-chunk 1 of chunk 4 from sub-chunk 2 of chunk 4 in chunk_index?
answer_key: How do you distinguish sub-chunk 1 of chunk 4 from sub-chunk 2 of chunk 4 in chunk_index?
notes: a question embedded inside a body paragraph, not a heading or bullet

question: Why does real LLM token count matter more than whitespace word count when deciding chunk size limits?
expected_answer_text: word count and token count diverge, sometimes significantly, and chunk-size limits in real systems are almost always expressed in tokens because that's what the embedding/LLM context window actually measures
answer_key: chunk-size limits in real systems are almost always expressed in tokens

question: How does a Python script pick up secrets that are stored in a .env file?
expected_answer_text: python-dotenv reads your .env file and loads its values into os.environ at runtime. After calling load_dotenv(), any key in .env is accessible via os.getenv() — exactly as if you had exported it in your shell.
answer_key: reads your .env file and loads its values into os.environ at runtime

question: In the Anthropic SDK, where does the system prompt go?
expected_answer_text: The system prompt is separate from messages[]. It sets the model's persona and behaviour for the entire conversation. In the Anthropic SDK it is a top-level parameter, not a message.
answer_key: In the Anthropic SDK it is a top-level parameter, not a message

question: What is the difference between the three ways of resetting a commit in git?
expected_answer_text: git reset --hard HEAD~1 discards changes permanently. Know the difference: --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed (default) keeps them unstaged, --hard discards everything.
answer_key: --soft keeps changes staged, --mixed (default) keeps them unstaged, --hard discards everything

question: Why doesn't a teammate get my commit-message check when they pull the project?
expected_answer_text: .git/hooks/ is NOT committed to the repo — it is local only. Every developer who clones the repo must set it up manually.
answer_key: .git/hooks/ is NOT committed to the repo — it is local only

question: Why run a package with python -m instead of pointing python at its __main__.py file?
expected_answer_text: python mypackage/__main__.py changes sys.path in a way that can break relative imports. python -m mypackage sets up sys.path correctly. Always use -m for packages.
answer_key: changes sys.path in a way that can break relative imports

question: When does the else block that follows a while loop actually run?
expected_answer_text: Python's while loop has an optional else clause. It runs when the loop ends naturally (condition becomes false), NOT when it ends via break.
answer_key: It runs when the loop ends naturally (condition becomes false), NOT when it ends via break

question: Why should each unit test build its own data instead of sharing one list with other tests?
expected_answer_text: If test_1 adds a message to a shared history list and test_2 reads from the same list, test_2 will fail or pass for the wrong reasons depending on test order. pytest does not guarantee order.
answer_key: test_2 will fail or pass for the wrong reasons depending on test order

question: What two things does assert_called_once_with() check?
expected_answer_text: assert_called_once_with() checks two conditions in one call: the mock was called exactly once (not zero times, not twice), AND it was called with the exact arguments you specify.
answer_key: the mock was called exactly once (not zero times, not twice), AND it was called with the exact arguments you specify

question: Why show the model a few solved examples before asking it the real question?
expected_answer_text: Provide 2-5 input/output examples before the new input. This encodes your definition of correct through examples, not descriptions — eliminating ambiguity.
answer_key: encodes your definition of correct through examples, not descriptions

question: Why does each LLM provider need its own code to pull the reply text out of the response?
expected_answer_text: The text is at data["message"]["content"], not data["content"][0]["text"] (Anthropic) or data["choices"][0]["message"]["content"] (OpenAI). Every provider has its own shape — this is exactly why the provider abstraction exists.
answer_key: Every provider has its own shape — this is exactly why the provider abstraction exists

question: Why set a time limit on requests to a model that runs on your own laptop?
expected_answer_text: timeout=120 — local models are slower than cloud APIs. Without a timeout, a large model could leave your program hanging indefinitely. 120 seconds is generous for llama3 on a MacBook.
answer_key: Without a timeout, a large model could leave your program hanging indefinitely

question: What is the only job of the function that sends one prompt to every provider?
expected_answer_text: It does not print anything. It does not save to disk. It does not catch exceptions (that is Day 4's job). Its single responsibility is: ask each provider, collect results, return the object.
answer_key: Its single responsibility is: ask each provider, collect results, return the object

question: What is conftest.py and why don't you import it?
expected_answer_text: conftest.py is a special pytest file that runs automatically before any tests in the same folder. You do not import it — pytest finds and executes it on its own.
answer_key: conftest.py is a special pytest file that runs automatically before any tests in the same folder

question: Why does saving a record that contains a date crash when you write it as JSON?
expected_answer_text: That dict looks fine until it hits json.dumps() — JSON has no native date type, so the encoder has nothing to convert a datetime into, and the call crashes.
answer_key: JSON has no native date type, so the encoder has nothing to convert a datetime into

question: Why is the model's reply more expensive than the prompt you send it?
expected_answer_text: Input tokens are processed once, in parallel, as the model reads your prompt. Output tokens are generated one at a time, sequentially — each new token requires a full forward pass through the model conditioned on everything generated so far.
answer_key: Output tokens are generated one at a time, sequentially — each new token requires a full forward pass

question: What do you give up in exchange for the Batch API discount?
expected_answer_text: In exchange for accepting results within a longer window — typically up to 24 hours rather than seconds — both providers currently offer roughly a 50% discount on both input and output tokens.
answer_key: accepting results within a longer window — typically up to 24 hours rather than seconds

question: What does defaultdict(list) do when you read a key that does not exist yet?
expected_answer_text: defaultdict(list) — a dict subclass where reading a missing key creates it with an empty list instead of raising KeyError.
answer_key: a dict subclass where reading a missing key creates it with an empty list instead of raising KeyError

question: After installing my package for development, why do code changes show up without reinstalling it?
expected_answer_text: Running pip install -e . reads that file and creates an editable install — Python treats the package as installed, but the code still lives in your working folder, so edits show up immediately with no reinstall step.
answer_key: Python treats the package as installed, but the code still lives in your working folder

question: Why can't you read a Word document with a plain open() call?
expected_answer_text: A .docx file is not a text file — it's a ZIP archive containing XML. Opening one with open(path).read() gets you binary garbage, not paragraphs.
answer_key: A .docx file is not a text file — it's a ZIP archive containing XML

question: Why compare two embeddings by their angle rather than by the plain distance between them?
expected_answer_text: Raw Euclidean distance would penalize that length difference even though the meaning matches. Cosine similarity ignores magnitude entirely and measures only the angle between two vectors.
answer_key: Raw Euclidean distance would penalize that length difference even though the meaning matches

question: Is it better to turn all the text pieces into vectors in one go or one at a time?
expected_answer_text: model.encode() accepts a list of strings just as happily as a single string, returning a 2D array (one row per input) instead of a 1D one — embedding every chunk in one call is both simpler and far faster than looping and calling .encode() once per chunk.
answer_key: embedding every chunk in one call is both simpler and far faster than looping

question: What goes wrong if a keyword score just adds up how often each search word appears?
expected_answer_text: Common words like "the" or "a" appear constantly and would dominate the score without carrying any real information about relevance. And a long document scores higher than a short one purely by containing more words overall.
answer_key: Common words like "the" or "a" appear constantly and would dominate the score

question: Why must the stored text and the user's question be split into words in exactly the same way?
expected_answer_text: Both indexing and querying need to split text into words the exact same way, or a query term that's technically "the same word" as one in a document will fail to match due to casing or punctuation.
answer_key: will fail to match due to casing or punctuation

question: Why can't the semantic score and the keyword score simply be added together?
expected_answer_text: This breaks immediately because the two scores don't live on the same scale. Chroma's cosine similarity is bounded, roughly 0 to 1 for normalized embeddings. BM25 is unbounded.
answer_key: This breaks immediately because the two scores don't live on the same scale

question: How does Reciprocal Rank Fusion score a chunk?
expected_answer_text: RRF scores a chunk using only the position it holds in each ranked list it appears in — never the raw score.
answer_key: RRF scores a chunk using only the position it holds in each ranked list it appears in

question: How does LangChain's v1 documentation define an agent?
expected_answer_text: The current (v1, 2026) definition LangChain's own docs give is blunt: "an agent is a model calling tools in a loop until a given task is complete."
answer_key: an agent is a model calling tools in a loop until a given task is complete

question: What state does search() keep between two calls?
expected_answer_text: rag_notes has no memory of any kind today -- search() is a pure, stateless function: same query in, same ranked chunks out, no awareness that a previous call ever happened.
answer_key: search() is a pure, stateless function: same query in, same ranked chunks out

question: What does a model tend to do when the passages it was given don't fully answer the question?
expected_answer_text: A model “wants” to be helpful, and if the retrieved context doesn't fully answer the question, it will often quietly fill the gap from its own training knowledge — which breaks the entire premise of “this answer came from your notes.”
answer_key: it will often quietly fill the gap from its own training knowledge

question: What happens to the listed sources when the assistant answers that it doesn't know?
expected_answer_text: Dropping them would be misleading in the other direction — pretending nothing was retrieved when something was, just not enough. Keeping them is the honest choice: they're the real chunks retrieval found and handed to the model.
answer_key: Keeping them is the honest choice: they're the real chunks retrieval found and handed to the model

question: Why is recall@k not enough on its own to judge how well a retriever ranks?
expected_answer_text: Recall@k treats a relevant chunk at rank 1 exactly the same as one at rank k — both just count as a hit. That hides a real quality difference.
answer_key: Recall@k treats a relevant chunk at rank 1 exactly the same as one at rank k

question: Why is an empty list a risky default value for a function parameter?
expected_answer_text: Python default argument values are evaluated once, at function-definition time — not on every call. A mutable default (a list) is shared across every call that doesn't pass its own value.
answer_key: Python default argument values are evaluated once, at function-definition time — not on every call

question: Why can't a generated answer be checked with a simple string comparison against the expected text?
expected_answer_text: Every golden entry has an expected_answer_text, but two correct answers can be worded completely differently. A == or in string check would mark the second one wrong. You need something that understands meaning, not characters.
answer_key: two correct answers can be worded completely differently

question: What is a typing.Protocol?
expected_answer_text: A Protocol is a class that declares a shape -- method names, parameters, return types -- without any implementation.
answer_key: A Protocol is a class that declares a shape -- method names, parameters, return types -- without any implementation

question: What changes when retrieval becomes an object instead of a function you pass the index to every time?
expected_answer_text: search(retrieval_index, query, n, mode) always takes the index as its first argument -- there's no object you can just call .search(query) on. The Protocol flips that: a Retriever is something that already knows its own index and only needs a query.
answer_key: a Retriever is something that already knows its own index and only needs a query

question: Why does the project have two dependency files instead of one?
expected_answer_text: Runtime deps (requirements.txt) — needed to run the app. Dev deps (requirements-dev.txt) — only needed in development and CI (ruff, pytest).
answer_key: Dev deps (requirements-dev.txt) — only needed in development and CI
